chapter: Bunk Johnson and American Music records
title: Russell's own wartime recordings of Bunk and George Lewis
summary: One long block on his cheap machines, the 1943 and 1944 sessions, the missing pianist at the Gypsy Tea Room, wrong speeds, and Ewing Nunn.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: He hadn't thrown them out fortunately, but he probably would have very soon if Dave hadn't gotten back. He could have thrown them in a wastebasket. So he thought it was just a joke, you know, that he sent something to amuse him. So Dave said, no, that's the real thing. It had to be worked on and issued. So anyway, I decided after that that I couldn't do much worse. So I got a machine. My machine only cost about $40. My brother put a little secondhand machine together and then bought an amplifier. My brother was a good electrical engineer in Pittsburgh where I was living during the war. So the first year I recorded the George Lewis climax records. And if anything, they did come out, I guess, the worst recording in a lot of ways. As you can tell from some of them, the bad starts that we get and some of them had to fade out. I had so much trouble with the needle, the cutting needle, sort of bouncing, jumping along due to some kind of a vibration. It's very peculiar. I still have some of those masters. Unbelievable looks when you look at the records. So my guess that I couldn't do any worse was almost wrong there. But the music came out pretty good on its climax. I sold them to Blue Note. Put them on a non-union climax label, it was. Because none of the guys at that time belonged to the union. Except the funny thing is, there was supposed to be a pianist on there, Walter Deku. They'd been on the Bunk records. This was 1943, I'm talking about now. And I came down here. First, I was supposed to record Bunk that year. I'd been writing to him about recording. Then about a week before I came down here, I was working for the same transformer company. My brother was out. He was the chief engineer, and I was just working in the test department. So the whole factory would close down for one week, and everybody had to take their vacation at that time. So anyway, a week before I was due for my vacation to come down here and record, my Bunk suddenly went to San Francisco. That's when he went out there. Rudy Blasher had a concert called This Is Jazz. And he'd appeared at the museum. He later played weekly sessions there, called the CIO Room. Well anyway, I went out then to San Francisco to hear that concert, because they had Ori's band to come up from California with Mud Carry. And others to play with Bunk. So I did record Bunk playing informally with Bertha Gonsolin, a pianist. A lady who'd come from New Orleans. She'd been out there. She'd even played a few dates with Oliver in 1922 or so, when Oliver was out there. So then I came on to San Francisco, I came on to New Orleans and recorded George Lewis then, which I'd hoped would be something that fit the issue commercially. Recording-wise, it was pretty bad, but the music was very good. It was George's first session under his own name, and they were really going good that day. With Kid Howard, his lip was in good shape, and Jim and all played well. But we were supposed to have a pianist, the same pianist that played with Bunk the year before, Walter Deku. And unfortunately, he was a member of the union. We did this over at a place called the Gypsy Tea Room. It had been called the Japanese Tea Room until we got in the war, and they had to change the name real quick. So a great big nightclub room. In front of it was a bar, a little room in front of the bar. And it turned out the union, I don't know what it would be called, the Board of Trustees or Executive Board or something of the union, was having their weekly or... At that time, they had both white and colored unions. And they were having their weekly meeting there in the... One corner of this big nightclub hall. So I guess Walter Deku came to the door and saw the union executives back there in the corner, so he never came in for the date. Which we didn't really miss the piano anyway, because most of the guys were used to playing without piano. In fact, George hadn't used the piano hardly ever in any of his jobs. Because the small clubs here, if they have a piano, if half of the keys will sound, they're all out of tune anyway, or too low when they can't tune up to it. And of course on parades, and they'd advertise on wagons, which they still did somewhat in those days, in the 40s even, why they'd be on trucks, of course. They didn't use piano. So all of the guys here always have been used and still are able to play without piano. So we didn't really miss the piano. But that's why there is no piano on there. So anyway, the next year I got another recording machine. It was also in pretty bad shape. I got it only one day before it came down here. We bought it secondhand for about, I don't remember the price, say $150 or something. And the turntable wouldn't even move. It was just sort of rusted, corroded into the thing. But my brother got it out some way and used emery paper and got it working very smoothly. And it worked very good mechanically, except it was the wrong speed. Everything was recorded at 81.6 in place of 78. And so everything came out sounding about a half a tone too low. If you play it back at 78, then you're playing it too slow. A lot of the records I issued had to be issued that way because when I'd have them mastered at some of the studios, New York, different places, where they could only play one speed if they had a, say, asynchronous motor that went according to how many cycles the current was going. So anyway, some of the recording of that wasn't too bad. But there again, I didn't know how to use the machine. I had a lot of trouble for thread even that second year. And I know Hugh Davis, who was the engineer that mastered most of those early bunk sides, complained bitterly that there were no highs at all. He said there was, I mean, no lows at all. Practically nothing below middle C, he said, on the thing. Of course, he was expecting, he'd been used to recording big bands like the Ellington Band and things. And it had a big bass section with maybe a couple of basses and piano and baritone, saxes and everything else. But let's see, all we had was the trombone, which a lot of times doesn't hardly go below middle C anyway. And the string bass, which unfortunately didn't pick up too well. But it wasn't a real heavy sounding bass anyway. But some of that recording wasn't too bad with that machine, actually. The next year I had the speed adjusted so that we could record a 78. But it was a pretty bad recording, actually, anybody would have to admit. Although I remember some of the numbers we did the next year, though, when Ewing Nunn, who's probably the most, I don't know what you'd say, the most engineer of anybody I know, a wonderful engineer. He's the son of the, he's still living, he's gone out of the business now. But he'd done probably the best recording I ever heard, as far as, he had the audiophile label. And he worked mostly in tape. He never did, he did have a disc machine at times he would use, though. But some of his recording was so good, I remember once I went into the studio once and I thought, surely there was a band playing in there, it turned out a tape machine. He would only record at 30 inches per minute, or per second, I mean, 30 inch speed, in place of 15 or like most of these machines.
